questions.stem:
A 55-year-old man has 2 months of cough, fevers and weight loss. A Gram stain of his sputum shows neutrophils and only faint, beaded, poorly staining structures that the technologist cannot call Gram positive or Gram negative. A second smear is stained with carbol fuchsin, heated, decolorized with acid alcohol and counterstained with methylene blue; it shows thin, slightly beaded rods that hold the fuchsia dye on a blue background.

Which property of this organism explains both staining results?
choices: A thick peptidoglycan layer that traps crystal violet after decolorization
A lipid-rich waxy wall of mycolic acids that resists both dye entry and removal
An outer membrane rich in lipopolysaccharide that loses crystal violet
A polysaccharide capsule that excludes both stains from the cell surface
The absence of a cell wall, which leaves only the cell membrane to stain

explain.html:
Mycobacteria are aerobic, non-motile bacteria that are technically Gram-positive rods but stain poorly on Gram stain. The reason is their thick, hydrophobic, waxy cell wall full of mycolic acids, which keeps ordinary dyes from getting in. The same wall is the basis for the acid-fast stain: carbol fuchsin is driven in (with heat in Ziehl-Neelsen, or by the Kinyoun method), and the waxy wall then holds the dye even through acid alcohol, so the bacilli look fuchsia on a blue background, the "red snappers." A fluorochrome (auramine-rhodamine) stain binds mycolic acids directly and is about 10 times more sensitive. The wall also makes mycobacteria resistant to drying.

This man's Gram stain showed faint beaded forms that would not commit to either color, and the carbol fuchsin smear showed thin beaded rods holding the fuchsia dye. One property, the mycolic acid wall, explains both results.
explain.table:
StainHow it worksAppearanceSensitivity
Ziehl-Neelsen or Kinyoun (carbol fuchsin)Waxy wall retains carbol fuchsin after acid alcoholFuchsia rods on blueAbout 104 organisms/mL
Fluorochrome (auramine-rhodamine)Dye binds mycolic acidsYellow-green on darkAbout 10 times more sensitive
Gram stainDyes poorly penetrate the waxy wallFaint, beaded, poorly stainingNot useful for mycobacteria
why: A thick peptidoglycan layer explains ordinary Gram positivity, but these organisms stained poorly and their acid fastness comes from mycolic acids.
A lipopolysaccharide outer membrane makes an organism Gram negative and has nothing to do with retaining carbol fuchsin.
Mycobacteria are defined by their waxy wall, not a capsule, and a capsule would not make them hold carbol fuchsin.
Mycobacteria have a very thick wall, and an organism without a wall could not retain carbol fuchsin.
explain.takeaway: Mycolic acids make the mycobacterial wall waxy, so the organisms stain poorly on Gram stain but retain carbol fuchsin through acid alcohol (acid fast).
explain.topic: Mycobacterial cell wall and acid-fast staining
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Understand Diagnostics for Mycobacterial Disease: AFB Stains

questions.stem:
A 71-year-old woman with bronchiectasis has a chronic cough. She was born in the United States and has no known TB exposure. Three sputum specimens are sent. Two show a few acid-fast bacilli on smear. A nucleic acid amplification test (Xpert MTB/RIF) on the first specimen is negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and a repeat on the second specimen is also negative. Cultures are pending.

Which of the following is the most likely interpretation of these results?
choices: Smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis that the nucleic acid test has missed
Pulmonary tuberculosis caused by a strain resistant to rifampin
A false-positive smear caused by contamination with stain precipitate
A nontuberculous mycobacterium rather than M. tuberculosis
Contamination of the sputum with dead tuberculosis organisms

explain.html:
A positive acid-fast smear shows mycobacteria but cannot separate M. tuberculosis (MTB) from nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM), so for infection control it is presumed MTB until shown otherwise. The nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT), such as Xpert MTB/RIF, is specific for MTB, with a very high positive predictive value and a good negative predictive value in respiratory samples. Read together, the two tests sort the patient: smear and NAAT both positive means MTB, NAAT positive with a negative smear still means MTB, and NAAT negative with a positive smear means presumptive NTM. Culture then names the species.

This woman has bronchiectasis, no TB exposure and was born in the US, two of her smears show AFB, and two NAATs are negative. In the US the incidence of NTM pulmonary disease is now higher than that of pulmonary TB, so this pattern points to NTM.
explain.table:
SmearNAATPresumptive reading
PositivePositiveMTB (over 95% positive predictive value)
NegativePositiveMTB
PositiveNegativeNTM
NegativeNegativeTB not excluded, but infectivity low
why: With enough organisms to be smear positive, the NAAT has a good negative predictive value and rarely misses MTB, and two NAATs were negative.
Xpert detects MTB whether or not a rifampin mutation is present, and it found no MTB at all.
Two separate specimens were smear positive, which argues against a staining artifact.
The NAAT detects DNA from dead organisms too, so dead MTB would still make it positive.
explain.takeaway: A positive AFB smear with a negative TB NAAT points to a nontuberculous mycobacterium, while a positive NAAT, even with a negative smear, points to M. tuberculosis.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Understand Diagnostics for Mycobacterial Disease: Molecular testing: Nucleic Acid Amplification Tests

questions.stem:
A 46-year-old man who keeps a large home aquarium has had a slowly enlarging, painless nodule on the back of his right hand for 6 weeks. New nodules have since appeared in a line up his forearm. He recalls scraping the hand while cleaning the tank. Biopsy shows granulomas, and an acid-fast stain shows a few bacilli. Culture at the lower temperature requested by the lab grows a mycobacterium after 2 weeks. His wife asks whether she could catch it from him.

Which of the following is true of this organism?
choices: It is a member of the tuberculosis complex and spreads by droplet nuclei
It lives in the environment and is not passed from person to person
It grows within 7 days on routine bacterial media as a rapid grower
It requires a human reservoir and passes between household members
It cannot be cultured and is diagnosed only by skin biopsy appearance

explain.html:
Mycobacteria fall into three groups. The MTB complex (MTB, M. bovis, M. africanum) causes tuberculosis, has human reservoirs and spreads through the air, which makes it a public health concern. Nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) are ubiquitous in water and soil, form biofilms at water and surface interfaces, and have no human or animal reservoir, so there is no person-to-person transmission. The third group, the non-cultivatable mycobacteria, includes M. leprae. Among the slower-growing NTM, M. marinum is linked to fish tanks and aquariums.

This man scraped his hand cleaning an aquarium and now has a granulomatous nodule with new nodules tracking up the forearm, and a mycobacterium grew slowly at a lower temperature. That is M. marinum, an environmental NTM, so his wife is not at risk from him.
explain.table:
GroupExamplesReservoir and spreadGrowth
MTB complexMTB, M. bovis (BCG), M. africanumHuman; airborne person to personSlow (2 to 8 weeks)
NTMMAC, M. kansasii, M. marinum, rapid growersWater and soil; no person-to-person spreadRapid (under 7 days) to slow
Non-cultivatableM. lepraeCauses leprosyCannot be cultured
why: The TB complex spreads by the airborne route from human cases, while this is an environmental NTM from an aquarium.
It needed 2 weeks to grow, which fits a slower grower, not a rapid grower under 7 days.
NTM have no human reservoir and do not pass between household members.
It grew in culture; the non-cultivatable mycobacterium is M. leprae.
explain.takeaway: Nontuberculous mycobacteria live in water and soil with no human reservoir, so they do not spread person to person; M. marinum is linked to fish tanks.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
Over 3 months, six patients who had cosmetic surgery at the same outpatient center develop draining wound infections that fail to improve on cephalexin. Routine bacterial cultures grow long, filamentous Gram-positive rods within 5 days, first dismissed as contaminants. An acid-fast stain of the wound drainage shows long, beaded, filamentous acid-fast rods. An inspection finds that instruments were rinsed in tap water after sterilization.

Which organism group is most likely responsible?
choices: Slow-growing Mycobacterium avium complex
Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex
The non-cultivatable Mycobacterium leprae
Pigmented slow growers such as M. kansasii
Rapid-growing nontuberculous mycobacteria

explain.html:
Mycobacteria are traditionally sorted by growth rate on solid media: rapid growers in under 7 days, intermediate growers in 1 to 2 weeks, and slow growers in 2 to 8 weeks, a group that includes MTB and MAC. Rapid-growing NTM, such as M. abscessus, M. chelonae and M. fortuitum, look atypical on AFB stain: longer and filamentous, unlike the small beaded rods of MTB. They may grow on routine bacterial media, where they appear as filamentous Gram-positive rods and are easily mistaken for contaminants. Their disease associations include pulmonary, focal and disseminated infection and clusters of surgical wound infections.

Six cosmetic surgery patients have draining wounds, routine cultures grew filamentous Gram-positive rods in 5 days, and the AFB stain shows long filamentous acid-fast rods. With instruments rinsed in tap water, a water-dwelling rapid grower is the culprit.
explain.table:
Growth groupTime on solid mediaExamples
Rapid growersUnder 7 daysM. abscessus, M. chelonae, M. fortuitum
Intermediate growers1 to 2 weeks
Slow growers2 to 8 weeksMTB, MAC, M. kansasii, M. marinum
Non-cultivatableNo growthM. leprae
why: MAC is a slow grower and mainly a lung or disseminated pathogen, so it would not grow in 5 days.
MTB is a slow grower that takes weeks and is not linked to instrument-borne wound clusters.
M. leprae cannot be cultured at all, and these grew in 5 days.
M. kansasii is a pigmented slow grower that would take weeks.
explain.takeaway: Rapid-growing NTM grow in under 7 days, can appear on routine media as filamentous Gram-positive rods, look long and filamentous on AFB stain, and cause surgical wound clusters.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 49-year-old man with alcohol use disorder and poor nutrition is started on a single drug for latent TB infection that blocks synthesis of a lipid unique to the mycobacterial wall. He was not given any supplement with it. After 2 months he reports burning and tingling in both feet that is slowly rising up his shins. His liver enzymes are mildly elevated. He has taken the drug as prescribed.

Which of the following would most likely have prevented his new symptom?
choices: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) given with each dose
Folic acid given with each dose
Monthly visual and color vision testing
Taking each dose with a high-fat meal
Monthly measurement of serum uric acid

explain.html:
Isoniazid (INH) inhibits mycolic acid synthesis and is active against replicating organisms in all tissues; it is metabolized in the liver with few drug interactions. Its two main toxicities are hepatitis and peripheral neuropathy. Mild chemical hepatitis is common (10 to 20%), clinical hepatitis is rare, and risk rises with age, alcohol and chronic hepatitis. The neuropathy is uncommon and dose related, and vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) helps prevent it, which is why the drug is paired as INH plus B6. On latent TB treatment, monitoring covers both hepatotoxicity and neurotoxicity.

This man with alcohol use disorder and poor nutrition took single-drug INH for latent infection without a supplement and now has ascending burning in his feet, with mildly elevated liver enzymes. Pyridoxine with each dose would most likely have prevented the neuropathy.

DrugMechanismKey adverse effectsResistance gene
IsoniazidInhibits mycolic acid synthesisHepatitis, peripheral neuropathy (prevent with B6)katG, inhA
Rifampin (rifamycins)RNA polymeraseOrange fluids, rash, flu-like illness; induces P450 and P-glycoproteinrpoB
PyrazinamideSemi-dormant organisms at acid pHHepatotoxicity, high uric acid and gout, arthralgiapnc
EthambutolCell wall (arabinogalactan) synthesisDose-dependent optic neuritis; renal dose adjustmentembB
why: Folic acid is not what protects against INH neuropathy; vitamin B6 is.
Visual acuity and color vision testing is for ethambutol optic neuritis.
Taking the drug with food does not prevent neuropathy.
Uric acid monitoring belongs to pyrazinamide, which causes hyperuricemia and gout.
explain.takeaway: Isoniazid inhibits mycolic acid synthesis and causes hepatitis and a dose-related peripheral neuropathy that vitamin B6 prevents.

questions.stem:
A 57-year-old man starts four-drug therapy for culture-proven pulmonary tuberculosis. After 3 weeks he develops sudden severe pain, swelling and redness of the first metatarsophalangeal joint of his left foot. Joint aspiration shows needle-shaped crystals. Serum uric acid is 10.4 mg/dL (normal 3.5 to 7.2). His clinician considers stopping the responsible drug but worries about how that would change the length of his treatment.

Stopping the drug most likely responsible would have which effect on his treatment?
choices: It would lose activity against organisms in the central nervous system
It would leave the regimen unable to block mycolic acid synthesis
It would remove the drug that hedges against isoniazid resistance
It would lose the drug that shortens the total course to 6 months
It would remove the only drug in the regimen that is bactericidal

explain.html:
The standard regimen for drug-susceptible TB is RIPE: rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for a 2-month initial phase, then isoniazid and rifampin in the continuation phase. Each drug has a role. INH and rifampin are the best drugs, ethambutol is the hedge against INH resistance, and pyrazinamide (PZA), which acts on semi-dormant organisms inside cells at acid pH, gives more rapid sterilization. If rifampin plus PZA are given in the first 2 months, the total course can be 6 months; without them, the minimum duration is 9 months.

This man developed acute gout of the first MTP joint with needle-shaped crystals and a uric acid of 10.4 three weeks into therapy, and PZA is the drug that raises uric acid and causes gout. Stopping it would take away the drug that makes a 6-month course possible.
explain.table:
Drug in RIPEWhy it is there
RifampinMost important drug; cidal for replicating and semi-dormant organisms
IsoniazidCidal against replicating organisms in all tissues
PyrazinamideFaster sterilization; with rifampin in months 1 to 2, allows a 6-month course
EthambutolHedge in case of isoniazid resistance
why: CNS activity is not what PZA contributes, and ethambutol is the drug noted for poor CNS penetration.
Mycolic acid synthesis is blocked by isoniazid, which is not the drug causing gout.
Ethambutol, not PZA, is the hedge against isoniazid resistance.
Isoniazid and rifampin are also bactericidal, so PZA is not the only one.
explain.takeaway: Pyrazinamide raises uric acid and can cause gout, and when given with rifampin in the first 2 months it allows a 6-month course instead of at least 9 months.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Treatment of TB Disease: Treatment Regimens

questions.stem:
A 64-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease has been on four-drug therapy for pulmonary tuberculosis for 7 weeks. Her drug doses were never adjusted for her kidney function. She reports blurry vision in both eyes and says that colors have started to look washed out. Visual acuity has dropped from 20/20 to 20/60 in both eyes. Fundus examination is normal.

Which drug is most likely responsible, and why was she at higher risk?
choices: Isoniazid, because it is metabolized by hepatic acetylation
Rifampin, because it induces cytochrome P450 enzymes
Ethambutol, because it is cleared by the kidneys
Pyrazinamide, because it raises the serum uric acid
Rifabutin, because it accumulates in the lens of the eye

explain.html:
Ethambutol inhibits cell wall synthesis, is active against replicating organisms, and is usually bacteriostatic, cidal only at high doses, with poor CNS penetration. Its key toxicity is retrobulbar (optic) neuritis, which is dose dependent, so patients have their visual acuity and red/green color discrimination monitored. Unlike isoniazid, rifampin and pyrazinamide, which depend on the liver for metabolism, ethambutol needs renal dosage adjustment.

This woman with chronic kidney disease has been on four-drug therapy for 7 weeks with doses never adjusted for her kidneys, and she now has blurred vision, washed-out colors and acuity down to 20/60 with a normal fundus. Ethambutol accumulated because her kidneys could not clear it, and the dose-dependent optic neuritis followed.
why: Isoniazid causes peripheral neuropathy and hepatitis, not optic neuritis, and its metabolism is hepatic.
Rifampin causes orange fluids, rash, a flu-like illness and drug interactions, not loss of color vision.
Pyrazinamide raises uric acid and causes gout, not vision loss.
Rifabutin is not linked to this visual picture.
explain.takeaway: Ethambutol causes dose-dependent optic neuritis with loss of acuity and color vision and is renally cleared, so its dose must be adjusted in kidney disease.
explain.subject: Microbiology

rows.if_right: a patient on isoniazid with burning feet and no B6

rows.why: Rifampin causes orange fluids, rash, a flu-like illness and drug interactions, not loss of color vision.

rows.if_right: a patient on four-drug therapy with acute gout

questions.stem:
A 39-year-old man with smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis and a large cavity on chest radiograph completes a 2-month initial phase of rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol under directly observed therapy. His isolate is fully susceptible. He feels better, but the sputum culture collected at the end of the 2 months still grows Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The team is planning his continuation phase with isoniazid and rifampin.

Which of the following is the most appropriate plan?
choices: Stop all drugs, because a full 2-month initial phase has been completed
Continue isoniazid alone, since the organisms are now in the dormant phase
Restart the same four drugs from day 1 for another 2-month initial phase
Switch to a second-line regimen because the culture shows drug resistance
Continue isoniazid and rifampin for a longer continuation phase

explain.html:
Treatment of drug-susceptible TB disease has two phases. The initial phase is 2 months of four drugs including rifampin and pyrazinamide, and the continuation phase is isoniazid and rifampin for 4 to 7 months. The aims are to rapidly cut the number of growing bacilli and to eradicate persisting bacilli for a durable cure, meaning no relapse. Patients at higher risk of relapse after the shorter course get a longer continuation phase, and the main reasons are cavitary disease plus a sputum culture still positive at 2 months, missing PZA plus rifampin in the initial phase, some extrapulmonary disease, and sometimes drug resistance.

This man has a large cavity and a positive 2-month culture, yet his isolate is fully susceptible and he took every dose under directly observed therapy. The plan is to continue isoniazid and rifampin for a longer continuation phase, not to stop, restart or change drugs.
why: The continuation phase is what eradicates persisting bacilli, so stopping after 2 months invites relapse.
TB disease is never treated with a single drug.
Repeating the initial phase is not the response; the continuation phase is lengthened.
His isolate is fully susceptible, so there is no resistance to act on.
explain.takeaway: Drug-susceptible TB is treated with a 2-month RIPE initial phase then isoniazid and rifampin, and cavitary disease with a positive 2-month culture calls for a longer continuation phase.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Treatment of TB Disease: Treatment Regimens

questions.stem:
A 52-year-old woman from Bangladesh has a positive interferon-gamma release assay found on employment screening. She has no symptoms, and her chest radiograph is normal. She drinks alcohol daily and has chronic hepatitis C with mildly elevated liver enzymes. She takes no other medications. Her clinician agrees that the benefits of treating her latent infection outweigh the risks and wants the regimen least likely to injure her liver.

Which regimen is most appropriate?
choices: Isoniazid daily for 9 months
Isoniazid daily for 6 months
Rifampin daily for 4 months
Rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol
Pyrazinamide and ethambutol for 2 months

explain.html:
Latent TB infection is treated with single or two-drug regimens. The preferred regimens are 3HP (isoniazid plus rifapentine once weekly for 3 months), 4R (rifampin daily for 4 months) and 3HR (isoniazid plus rifampin daily for 3 months); 6 or 9 months of isoniazid are alternatives. Monitoring follows each drug's toxicity. Isoniazid hepatitis rises with age (up to 2% at 50 to 64) and with underlying liver disease, alcohol and other hepatotoxins, while with rifampin the major concern is drug interactions.

This 52-year-old drinks daily and has chronic hepatitis C with abnormal enzymes, which stacks every isoniazid hepatitis risk factor, and she takes no other medications. Rifampin daily for 4 months is preferred, short and avoids isoniazid entirely, and with no other drugs its interaction problem does not apply.
explain.table:
LTBI regimenRankMain concern
3HP: isoniazid plus rifapentine weekly, 3 monthsPreferredLess hepatotoxicity than INH alone
4R: rifampin daily, 4 monthsPreferredDrug interactions
3HR: isoniazid plus rifampin daily, 3 monthsPreferredINH hepatitis, rifampin interactions
6H or 9H: isoniazid, 6 or 9 monthsAlternativeINH hepatitis and neuropathy
why: Nine months of isoniazid is an alternative regimen with the most isoniazid liver exposure.
Six months of isoniazid still carries isoniazid hepatitis risk in a woman who drinks and has liver disease.
Four drugs are for TB disease, not latent infection with a normal chest radiograph.
This is not a latent treatment regimen, and pyrazinamide is itself hepatotoxic.
explain.takeaway: Preferred LTBI regimens are 3HP, 4R and 3HR, and in a patient at high risk of isoniazid hepatitis, 4 months of rifampin avoids isoniazid.

questions.stem:
A 31-year-old woman with multidrug-resistant pulmonary tuberculosis is started on an all-oral 6-month regimen that includes linezolid, pretomanid and a diarylquinoline. The diarylquinoline was the first drug developed and approved specifically for MDR TB. Her team orders a baseline electrocardiogram and plans repeat tracings during therapy, along with liver tests.

The diarylquinoline acts on which target, and what is the reason for the ECG monitoring?
choices: Mycolic acid synthesis, because it can cause heart block
Bacterial RNA polymerase, because it can cause bradycardia
ATP synthase, because it can prolong the QT interval
NADH dehydrogenase, because it can cause atrial fibrillation
DNA gyrase, because it can cause ventricular hypertrophy

explain.html:
Antimycobacterial drugs hit several targets, and some sites of action are unique to mycobacterial agents: ATP synthase (bedaquiline), NADH dehydrogenase (clofazimine), intracellular acidification (pyrazinamide), arabinogalactan (ethambutol) and mycolic acids (isoniazid). Other targets are shared with ordinary antibiotics: RNA polymerase (rifamycins), DNA gyrase (fluoroquinolones) and the ribosome (aminoglycosides, linezolid). Bedaquiline is a diarylquinoline and the first drug developed and approved for MDR TB, and it is part of the 6-month bedaquiline, linezolid and pretomanid regimen.

Its toxicities are QT prolongation, hepatotoxicity, nausea and arthralgias, which is why this woman gets a baseline ECG, repeat tracings and liver tests.
why: Mycolic acid synthesis is the isoniazid target, and heart block is not the bedaquiline concern.
RNA polymerase is the rifamycin target, not a diarylquinoline target.
NADH dehydrogenase is the clofazimine target.
DNA gyrase is the fluoroquinolone target.
explain.takeaway: Bedaquiline, a diarylquinoline approved for MDR TB, inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase and prolongs the QT interval.
explain.subject: Microbiology

rows.if_right: a patient on clofazimine, the NADH dehydrogenase drug in MDR TB regimens

questions.stem:
A 44-year-old man from Peru is diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis after sputum smears and a nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) are positive. The NAAT reports no rifampin resistance mutation. He starts a standard four-drug regimen. After 6 weeks his cough has improved, and a resident proposes repeating the NAAT to show that the organisms have been killed, and canceling the cultures since the diagnosis is already confirmed.

Which of the following is the best response to this plan?
choices: Keep the cultures, which are needed for full drug susceptibility testing
Cancel the cultures, since the NAAT already excluded drug resistance
Repeat the NAAT, since a positive result will show rifampin resistance
Repeat the NAAT, since a negative result will confirm a cure
Cancel the cultures, since smears can track susceptibility

explain.html:
NAATs like Xpert MTB/RIF detect MTB DNA and most rifampin resistance mutations, and they speed early diagnosis. They have limits that shape how they are used. The NAAT detects DNA whether organisms are alive or dead, so it can stay positive after the bacilli are no longer viable; a positive NAAT is not repeated and cannot track response to treatment. It also looks only at rifampin resistance, and molecular tests do not know every resistance locus, so a negative molecular result does not exclude resistance. That is why, even with a positive NAAT, cultures are still needed for susceptibility data.

The resident's plan fails on both counts. A repeat NAAT could be positive from dead organisms and could never prove cure, and canceling cultures would throw away the only route to phenotypic susceptibility testing for isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol. Keep the cultures.
why: Xpert reports only rifampin resistance mutations and cannot exclude resistance to the other drugs.
A positive NAAT on therapy may come from dead organisms and says nothing new about resistance.
The NAAT detects DNA from dead organisms too, so it cannot confirm cure.
Smears count organisms and mark infectivity but give no susceptibility information.
explain.takeaway: A TB NAAT detects DNA from live or dead organisms and only most rifampin mutations, so it is not repeated to monitor therapy and cultures are still required for susceptibility testing.

questions.stem:
A 33-year-old woman with a kidney transplant on a calcineurin inhibitor for rejection prevention is diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis. She is started on four drugs, one of which turns her urine and tears orange. Two weeks later her calcineurin inhibitor level has fallen well below target despite unchanged dosing, and her creatinine is rising. The transplant team asks which TB drug could replace the culprit while keeping the regimen effective.

Which of the following is the best choice?
choices: Rifabutin, a rifamycin with less effect on drug-metabolizing enzymes
Rifapentine, a longer-acting rifamycin given once weekly
Ethambutol at a higher dose to make up for the lost rifamycin
Isoniazid at a higher dose to make up for the lost rifamycin
Pyrazinamide for a full 9 months in place of the rifamycin

explain.html:
The rifamycins (rifampin, rifabutin, rifapentine) act on the bacterial RNA polymerase (rpoB), are cidal for replicating and semi-dormant organisms, and rifampin is called the most important first-line drug. Their adverse effects include orange staining of body fluids, rash, a flu-like syndrome and occasional hepatotoxicity. The big practical problem is drug interactions: rifampin induces cytochrome P450 and P-glycoprotein transport, lowering the levels of many co-administered drugs. Rifabutin has less enzyme-inducing effect and can replace rifampin, keeping rifamycin activity in the regimen.

Orange tears and urine identify rifampin, and her calcineurin inhibitor level fell with a rising creatinine, a threat to her graft. Swapping to rifabutin solves the interaction while keeping the most important drug class.
why: Rifapentine is still a rifamycin inducer and does not solve the interaction.
Ethambutol is usually bacteriostatic and cannot stand in for the most important first-line drug.
Isoniazid is already in the regimen and cannot replace a rifamycin's activity.
Pyrazinamide earns its benefit together with rifampin in the first 2 months, not as a substitute for it.
explain.takeaway: Rifampin induces cytochrome P450 and P-glycoprotein and lowers levels of drugs such as calcineurin inhibitors, and rifabutin induces less and can replace it.

questions.stem:
Two patients are seen in a TB clinic on the same day. Patient 1 is an asymptomatic 25-year-old with a positive interferon-gamma release assay and a normal chest radiograph, who is started on a single drug. Patient 2 is a 50-year-old with a large right upper lobe cavity and smear-positive sputum, who is started on four drugs. A student asks why giving Patient 2 a single drug would be unsafe when it is acceptable for Patient 1.

Which of the following best explains the difference?
choices: Single drugs cannot penetrate a cavity, but they penetrate granulomas well
Patient 2's organisms are already resistant, while Patient 1's organisms are not
Combination therapy is used in disease to reduce toxicity by allowing lower doses
A cavity holds enough organisms that resistant mutants are present before therapy
Latent organisms are replicating faster and are killed before mutations can arise

explain.html:
Drug resistance in TB starts with spontaneous chromosomal mutations at a low, fixed rate: about 1 in 107 to 108 organisms for isoniazid and 1 in 108 to 109 for rifampin. A pulmonary lesion holds about 108 actively replicating organisms per mL, and a cavity up to 1011 per mL, so mutants resistant to any single drug are already present before treatment. One drug would kill the susceptible majority and select the resistant mutants. Resistance to both INH and rifampin at once needs both mutations in one organism, about 1 in 1015, which is why TB disease is always treated with multi-drug regimens. In latent infection the organism count is low (under 107) and not actively replicating, so single-drug therapy carries little risk.

Patient 2's large cavity holds a huge bacillary population, while Patient 1 has latent infection with very few organisms. Burden, not penetration or prior resistance, is the difference.
explain.table:
SettingOrganismsSpontaneous single-drug mutants present?Therapy
CavityUp to 1011 per mLYes (INH 1 in 107 to 108, RIF 1 in 108 to 109)Multi-drug regimen
Latent infectionUnder 107, not replicatingUnlikelyOne or two drugs
why: Penetration is not the reason; the size of the organism population is.
Nothing shows Patient 2's strain is resistant; the issue is pre-existing mutants within a large susceptible population.
TB drugs are combined to prevent resistance, not to lower doses and toxicity.
Latent organisms are few and not actively replicating, not fast growing.
explain.takeaway: TB disease is always treated with combinations because a large bacillary burden already contains spontaneously resistant mutants, while low-burden latent infection can be treated with one or two drugs.

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old man from Moldova presents with 3 months of cough and weight loss. He was treated for pulmonary tuberculosis 5 years ago, took his pills irregularly without observation, and stopped after 3 months when he felt better. Sputum smear is positive, and a nucleic acid amplification test detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis with a rifampin resistance mutation. Later culture-based testing shows resistance to rifampin and isoniazid and susceptibility to fluoroquinolones.

Which of the following best describes his tuberculosis?
choices: Mono-resistant TB acquired at the time of his first infection
Multidrug-resistant TB that was most likely acquired during therapy
Extensively drug-resistant TB that was most likely acquired during therapy
Pre-extensively drug-resistant TB acquired at the time of his first infection
Drug-susceptible relapse with a false-positive molecular resistance result

explain.html:
TB resistance has its own terms. Mono-resistant TB is resistant to any single drug, most often isoniazid. MDR TB is resistant to at least both isoniazid and rifampin. Pre-XDR is MDR plus fluoroquinolone resistance, and XDR is MDR plus fluoroquinolone resistance plus resistance to other key drugs. Resistance is primary when a person is infected with a resistant strain and secondary (acquired) when it develops during treatment. The main reasons to worry about MDR are prior treatment now relapsing, especially if not well monitored, contact with an MDR case and failure to respond to standard therapy.

This man took his first course irregularly, without observation, and stopped at 3 months, and now he has relapsed with resistance to rifampin and isoniazid but susceptibility to fluoroquinolones. That is MDR TB, most likely acquired during his poorly supervised treatment, which is exactly what directly observed therapy is meant to prevent.
explain.table:
TermDefinition
Mono-resistantResistant to any single drug (most often isoniazid)
MDRResistant to at least isoniazid and rifampin
Pre-XDRMDR plus fluoroquinolone resistance
XDRMDR plus fluoroquinolone resistance plus resistance to other key drugs
Primary resistanceInfected with a resistant strain
Secondary (acquired) resistanceDevelops during treatment
why: He is resistant to two drugs, not one, and his history points to resistance acquired on treatment.
XDR requires fluoroquinolone resistance plus other key drugs, and his isolate is fluoroquinolone susceptible.
Pre-XDR requires fluoroquinolone resistance, and his history points to acquired, not primary, resistance.
Culture-based testing confirmed the resistance, so it is not a false-positive molecular result.
explain.takeaway: MDR TB is resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampin, and irregular, unobserved prior treatment is the classic setting for acquired resistance.

questions.stem:
A 38-year-old woman who moved to the United States from Southeast Asia 2 years ago has 6 weeks of cough, night sweats, and weight loss. Chest radiograph shows a right upper lobe infiltrate without a cavity. Sputum smear shows acid-fast bacilli, and a nucleic acid amplification test (Xpert MTB/RIF) reports M. tuberculosis detected, rifampin resistance not detected. She starts rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol under directly observed therapy. At week 7 she has gained weight, and her sputum smear is negative. Phenotypic susceptibility testing on her culture now returns: resistant to isoniazid; susceptible to rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. A resident is puzzled because the molecular test reported no resistance.

Which statement best explains both the missed resistance and her good response?
choices: Pyrazinamide killed the replicating bacilli, so isoniazid was never needed in the regimen
The phenotypic isoniazid result is a false positive, since the molecular test is more accurate
Rifampin alone was enough, since spontaneous rifampin resistance does not occur in TB
The molecular test looks only for rifampin mutations; her other three drugs stayed active
Isoniazid resistance arose during therapy, after 7 weeks of exposure to the drug

explain.html:
Molecular tests for tuberculosis detect specific resistance mutations, so they are only as complete as the loci they examine. Xpert MTB/RIF detects MTB and most rifampin resistance mutations in rpoB; isoniazid resistance arises mainly in katG and inhA, which this test does not read, and a negative molecular result never completely excludes resistance. Phenotypic susceptibility testing in public health and reference labs takes up to 4 more weeks and remains the reference. This is why the standard initial regimen is four drugs: isoniazid and rifampin are the best drugs, pyrazinamide shortens the course, and ethambutol is the hedge if isoniazid resistance is present (about 10% of foreign-born and 5% of US-born cases).

In this patient the isolate was isoniazid resistant from the start (primary resistance), but during the initial phase rifampin and pyrazinamide carried the regimen, the combination that drives sterilization, and ethambutol added a third active drug, so rifampin was never effectively alone and resistant mutants were not selected. Her weight gain and smear conversion under directly observed therapy fit this. The clinical point: wait for full phenotypic results, and do not drop ethambutol before isoniazid susceptibility is known.
why: Pyrazinamide acts on semi-dormant intracellular organisms in acid pH and shortens the course; it does not stand in for isoniazid against replicating bacilli.
Phenotypic testing is the reference, and a molecular test cannot see resistance at genes it does not examine.
Spontaneous rifampin resistance occurs in about 1 in 108 to 109 organisms, enough to be present in active disease.
She improved on 7 weeks of observed four-drug therapy, which fits resistance present from infection rather than acquired on treatment.
explain.takeaway: Xpert MTB/RIF detects rifampin (rpoB) but not isoniazid (katG/inhA) resistance; with isoniazid inactive, rifampin and pyrazinamide carry the initial phase, and ethambutol ensures rifampin is not left with one partner.
explain.topic: Molecular resistance testing and the ethambutol hedge

explain.objective: Understand Diagnostics for Mycobacterial Disease: Antimicrobial Susceptibility and Resistance Testing

questions.stem:
A 46-year-old man has 3 weeks of fever, night sweats, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. His brother completed tuberculosis treatment last year. Chest radiograph shows a moderate right pleural effusion without parenchymal infiltrate or cavity. Three induced sputum specimens are smear negative for acid-fast bacilli, and two sputum nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT) are negative. Thoracentesis yields a lymphocyte-predominant exudate; pleural fluid acid-fast smear is negative and pleural fluid NAAT is negative. Mycobacterial cultures of sputum and pleural fluid are pending. The team plans to record that tuberculosis has been excluded.

Which interpretation of these results is most accurate?
choices: He must stay in airborne isolation until cultures return, since pleural TB spreads easily
Rifampin-resistant TB is likely, since resistant strains are missed by the NAAT
A nontuberculous mycobacterium is most likely, since every NAAT was negative
Tuberculosis is excluded, since NAAT has a good negative predictive value
Tuberculosis is still possible, since NAAT is less sensitive on pleural fluid

explain.html:
Nucleic acid amplification tests detect MTB DNA quickly, and their published performance comes mostly from respiratory samples, where positive predictive value is very high and negative predictive value is good. Used on other clinical specimens such as pleural fluid and CSF, NAAT keeps high specificity but has lower sensitivity and negative predictive value. Even in sputum, if NAAT and smear are both negative, TB is not excluded; the combination only means infectivity is low. Mycobacterial culture, which needs less processing for sterile sites and is held for 6 weeks, is what finally confirms or rules out the diagnosis.

This man has a household exposure, fever, night sweats, and a lymphocyte-predominant pleural exudate, a picture that keeps TB high on the list. His negative sputum results support low infectivity, but the negative pleural NAAT cannot rule out pleural TB. The right move is to keep TB open and follow the pleural and sputum cultures rather than closing the workup.
explain.table:
Result patternInterpretation
Respiratory NAAT and smear both positivePresume MTB (PPV above 95%)
Respiratory NAAT positive, smear negativePresumptive MTB
Respiratory NAAT negative, smear positivePresumptive NTM
Respiratory NAAT and smear both negativeTB not excluded, infectivity low
Pleural or CSF NAAT negativeTB not excluded (lower sensitivity and NPV)
why: Negative smears and two negative GeneXpert results indicate low infectivity and meet the criterion to stop airborne isolation.
Xpert detects MTB and reports rifampin mutations separately; resistance does not hide the organism.
The NTM rule applies when the smear is positive and the NAAT is negative; here the smears are negative.
The good NPV belongs to respiratory specimens; in pleural fluid sensitivity and NPV are lower, and both-negative results never exclude TB.
explain.takeaway: NAAT is highly specific but less sensitive on pleural fluid and CSF, so a negative result there does not exclude TB; culture remains the definitive test.
